front_page.headline: Decision models are now a category, not a curiosity
front_page.dek: TypeSafe’s Jev started it in September. This week OpenAI shipped a competitor to everyone.
front_page.body:
Most AI models you use are writers: you ask, they reply in sentences, and your code has to fish the answer out of the prose. A decision model skips the essay. You hand it messy input and it returns a typed answer, such as a category, a score or a route, plus how confident it is.

Think of a chat model as a consultant who writes you a memo, and a decision model as a referee who raises a flag and tells you how sure he is. For software that has to make thousands of calls a minute, the referee is what you want.

TypeSafe AI, founded by a former OpenAI researcher, came out of stealth on 16 September with Jev, pitched at high-volume work like classifying service requests, triaging alerts and reviewing AI agents’ output. On 22 October, TechCrunch reported that OpenAI has made its own decision model widely available.

Why it matters: the interesting number is the confidence score. It tells you when to let the model act alone and when to hand the case to a person, which is the hard part of every triage system.
front_page.fits: Fraud and outlier triage: classify, score, and route uncertain cases to a human.

front_page.headline: Block’s Dessa learned to talk without ever reading
front_page.dek: A voice model trained only on recorded conversations, small enough to run on a MacBook.
front_page.body:
Almost every voice assistant is a text model wearing a microphone. Dessa, from a small research lab at Block, was trained on recorded human conversations alone: no text and no pretrained model underneath.

It is full-duplex, meaning it listens while it talks, so it can be interrupted, say “yeah” while you speak, and match your timing, like a phone call rather than a walkie-talkie. Jack Dorsey announced it on 23 October.

You can’t use it yet. There is a waitlist, early access is going to AI safety researchers, and there are no weights, benchmarks or pricing. If you want to try a full-duplex model today, Kyutai’s Moshi has open weights.

my_stack.headline: Claude Haiku 5.5 launches with very low prices for short prompts
my_stack.dek: Two price bands: cheap under 100,000 tokens, more above it.
my_stack.body:
Reported pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, rising above that. The same report says Sonnet 5.5 cache reads were cut too.

For high-volume steps like scoring, routing and summarizing, this changes which model is worth using. Check Anthropic’s pricing page before you budget.
my_stack.fits: Cheap high-volume classification steps inside agents.

my_stack.headline: Claude Duet opens a waitlist

my_stack.body: TechCrunch describes Duet as Anthropic’s bet on agents. Access is waitlist only for now, so there is nothing to test yet.
my_stack.fits: Agentic engineering: worth reading how Anthropic packages agents for users.

my_stack.headline: uv and ty are coming together
my_stack.dek: Astral is joining its Python package manager and its type checker.
my_stack.body: If you already use uv, this is the one to read: one tool that installs, runs and type-checks your Python. Details are in Astral’s post.
my_stack.fits: Python tooling for every project in the plan.

paper_of_the_day.title: Left alone with nothing to do, AI agents started playing
paper_of_the_day.authors: MIT researchers, as reported by TechCrunch
paper_of_the_day.summary:
Researchers left 13 AI agents on a virtual island with no assigned task. The agents invented games and rituals, and, according to the report, got better at their actual jobs afterwards.

The preview links the news coverage. Real editions link the paper itself.
paper_of_the_day.why_it_matters: Multi-agent systems behave differently over long runs than in short tests. If you run agents for hours, evaluate them over hours.

try_this_today.title: Price your classification step on a cheaper model
try_this_today.why: Cheap models change the math for any agent step that sorts, scores or routes.
steps: Pick one classification step in an agent you run, and 100 real examples with known right answers.
Run them through the model you use now and record accuracy, tokens and cost.
Run the same 100 through the cheapest current model.
Write down one line: accuracy change, cost change. That line is a post for your site.

hype_check.claim: TypeSafe says Jev is far faster and cheaper than general LLMs on business workflows.
hype_check.explanation: TypeSafe itself noted the workflows were designed by its own team. Promising, but test it on your own data before believing the multiplier.

hype_check.claim: Microsoft says its AI beat doctors on hard diagnostic cases.
hype_check.explanation: The study is in Science, but TechCrunch’s coverage questions where most of the improvement comes from. Read the details before quoting the headline.
